Messages.Author: Tom Duncan
Messages.Body:
Personally, I am. I have always thought that the other creatures of the
WoD should be subjected to a methuselah's whim directly from the crypt.
I am looking forward to seeing how the alternate crypt cards are
handled in the hunter's set. If all goes well, I think it's likely that
we will see others - after all, their is no new material for oWoD.
Farming it deeper is the only way to continue to expand VtES. If ever
there are 'other creature' crypt possibilities, we may see something
similar to the Scarce trait on them to keep them from being the focus
of crypts, or even a VEKN tournament rule similar to the storyline

with alien telepathy and cybernetic weapons, so long as it is balanced
and playable. I say the more the merrier.

Messages.Author: jnew...@difsol.com
Messages.Body:
as...@hotmail.com wrote:
> So, we are getting hunter crypt cards. What is next? Werewolf crypt
> cards? Mage crypt cards? Wraith crypt cards? Changeling crypt cards?
> Mummy crypt cards? and so on. Do you guys look forward to this?

Not terribly much looking forward to most of the others - at least, not
enough to build a full Mage deck or whatever. Hunters, though, make
sense.

All the other supernaturals in WoD were pretty much tangential to the
role of VtM (possible exception of Wraiths interacting with Giovanni,
but that's not wraiths in general or vampires in general). Individual
Garou, wraiths, etc. can be recurited to assist a methuselah in their
eternal struggle, but as a group, all the other supernaturals are
pretty insular and have their own concerns oustide the existence of
vampire (or each others', or mortal) society. The various kinds much
prefer (as a group) to ignore each other altogether and handle their
own problems.

Hunters, on the other hand, are all about getting in-your-face with
everybody else. Hunter lore is chock full of Hunters being manipulated
by vampires. Manipulating and escaping Hunters is an important part of
kindred survival. Heck, manipulating non-hunter mortals would be quite
in-theme of a Vampire game. This is most certainly something that
vampires do, all the time, and adding it to the game makes perfect
thematic sense.

If a methuselah is now able to influence only mortal minions to defeat
his opponents in the Jyhad, more power to him. This is something that
would probably be unheard of in the past, but with the advent of Imbued
Hunters, who have supernatural powers that most Kindred don't really
understand, it's may be possible for a quick-thinking methuselah to
pull it off. This is also thematically appropriate.

> I myself is kinda uncertain. On one hand - VtES is a VERY good
> game-mechanic, and it deserves to be used more "widely" then just with
> vampires.
>
> On the other hand - I seriously hope WW is sensitive with the mix
> between the different Awakened, so that the wraiths don´t have votes
> in Kindred referendum and so on (it´s bad enough that Sabbat vamps can
> vote to decide who become Camarilla princes).

I might get queasy if they added enough crypt-influenceable mages (or
garou, or whatever) to make a whole deck around them work well. I might
not. But Hunters are too appropriate to the themes and background for
me to get worked up over.

John

Messages.Author: flan
Messages.Body:
as...@hotmail.com wrote:
> So, we are getting hunter crypt cards. What is next? Werewolf crypt
> cards? Mage crypt cards? Wraith crypt cards? Changeling crypt cards?
> Mummy crypt cards? and so on. Do you guys look forward to this?

I don't see anything special about Hunters that makes them any more or
less acceptable than other cards previously represented by allies to
have in the crypt. But then I don't know any canon, either...

> On the other hand - I seriously hope WW is sensitive with the mix

> between the different Awakened, so that the wraiths don愒 have votes
> in Kindred referendum and so on (it愀 bad enough that Sabbat vamps can

> vote to decide who become Camarilla princes).

The way I think about it, not knowing any better, is that a Hunter is
mechanically a Vampire, with some special, and "Cannot play cards
requiring a Vampire" on the bottom. Maybe some disciplines that they
can play as a vampire, but otherwise excluding them from this huge range
of cards.

Each time some new game concept is put in place that segregates groups
of cards (Grouping, Sects, Anarchs/Black Hand, &c, &c) it subdivides the
groups of cards and effects out there to make it less likely that some
new added card will have an overpowered interaction, without saying "You
can't play this expansion with that expansion." It's a good thing. I
think of this the same way - it makes it possible to make new cards,
probably small cards, to bring out from the crypt, without being prone
to weenie-abuse. It's very hard to add small support vamps that are
useable to boost diverse, larger-capacity crypts, without giving weenie
decks even more ammunition. By stripping away Vampire-ness, it hems in
some potential abuses. By leaving them vulnerable to all the effects
that can subvert allies generally (if they are), they are checked in a
way that small vampires aren't - which means you can also give them more
interesting and unique abilities or cards.

I'm a fan of diversity. And small sets, where I can feel like I can
pick and choose which aspects of the game I want to emphasize more. I'm
sure I'll wind up buying singles or trading for the LOB cards that I
want. I'm sure I'll buy a bunch of Reckoning if it looks interesting.

Messages.Author: Screaming Vermillian
Messages.Body:


The above isn't a problem in the NWoD as it was initially designed with
this in mind (no one 'world' of supernaturalizm living in exclusion to
others). The only thing WoD: Chicago assists is in trying to figure out
the character motivations and relationships between all of these
factions. THAT'S about as tough as figuring out the dynamics of the
CCGs disciplines interacting with one another.

> Perhaps we'll be seeing this same sort of fusion in V:TES as well.

Perhaps, but VTES wasn't initially built with this in mind. The
mechanics of the game and previous cards (which refer to 'vampire' when
really, other things would have worked too) don't interact nicely with
other supernaturals. Using blood for a payment system in vampire might
not translate nicely to mages, or werewolves. Political referendums (a
third of the current game, kind of) doesn't translate well, fluff wise,
to other supernaturals (though in NWoD mages, werewolves and kindred
may all share the same counsel).

In short there are problems with VTES mechanically, and with VTM,
fluffily. Granted, one thing at a time, and I'm sure the bridges can be
gapped. (like, starting with hunters).

~SV

MathiasTCK wrote:
> When it's a short response to a short post, I don't see the need..

'Cause people have no idea what you are talking about if there is no
context. Just calling things out into the air means nothing if no one
knows what you are calling out about.

>If whatever news group reader people are using is inferior to google
> groups in this fashion then why are they using it?

This is usenet. Usenet existed looooong before google groups. Usenet is
intended to be used by newsreaders. Google groups is currently a
convinient web interface for folks who don't have newsreaders. But the
majority of people who read usenet use newsreaders. Some newsreaders
thread discussions. Some don't. But that is irrelevant. If you want
people to know what you are talking about in any text medium, be it
usenet, a web bbs, or google groups, it is a good idea to quote
relevant text that you are replying to. As it makes the conversation
make more sense for everyone.

And if you don't quote relevant text, people tend to be annoyed and
just ignore you.

> Plus depending on someone else's quotes loses track of the larger
> conversation. The conversation starts ignoring what people don't
> quote, which is silly.

So the answer to this is to just have everyone shouting randomly into a
void?

> If you want to respond to a specific part, of a large post, and what
> you are saying makes no sense without context, then I can see why you
> would need to quote.

And if you want people to have any idea of what you are talking about,
it is also a good idea to use a quote. And if you want people to pay
attention to what you are saying, it is also a good idea use a quote.

> The majority does agree though, and it is polite to follow the
> conventions of said majority in a public forum.

Its about much more than politeness. I'd think that people would want
others to read their posts and pay attention to them, and then respond
to them.

If you don't quote relevant text and provide a context, people tend to
ignore you, as it is often too much work to try and figure out what you
are talking about.

-Peter

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
MathiasTCK wrote:

> The Lasombra wrote:
>>Because two weeks from now your post that has no context will be
>>completely worthless as far as understanding any topic of discussion.
>
> How is it worthless if any user can just view one message up in the
> tree to see what they are responding to?

Faulty premise -- it is not true that "any user" can just "view up"
one message in the tree.

ATM (since I am reading and posting via my personal ISP's news server),
I cannot "view up" the whole tree for this conversation, for example.

>>Every post should be able to stand on its own, and be understood.
>
> Yeah that's what I'm asking, why can't we expect people to be able to
> view one step up in the tree?

Because that's not how USENET works.

It's how Google works.

USENET (for which Google offers a gateway and an archive, but doesn't
replace) is a medium for transmission and *temporary* storage of "posts"
(basically a grown-up mailing list with slight latency and retention
add-ons).

See also replying to email.
Just because you can see the whole conversation (because you're using gmail,
for example) doesn't mean the recipient can (even if his email address
ends in "@gmail.com"). Or that the onus for digging out context should
fall on the recipient rather than the sender, even if he does have the
ability.

That's why gmail includes context by default, and why google groups
should as well.

But just because google groups has a shortcoming in that regard doesn't
mean you have to accept it -- you can quote context with a slight bit
of additional effort.

> I think anything that creates a barrier to entry is bad for a group.

True, but this convention does not create a barrier to entry.

> Any unnecessary rule is bad, etc.

True, but the convention is not unnecessary.

newsreader can't handle threaded messages, use Google Groups for
christ's sake. If a newsreader can't handle threaded messages, and it
can't hold onto old posts (or at least download them to display when
you're reading a message from the thread), then I say your newsreader
sucks. And if you're actually setting your newsreader to delete old
posts and to never download any posts other than what you're reading, I
have to ask, why? An 80 GB hard-drive costs less than a 40MB drive
used to be. Dial-up connections are fast disappearing entirely. The
bandwidth and storage space required for a USENET post isn't what it
used to be, in comparison to the capacity that most people have for
storing or downloading those posts. Quoting posts is still a good
idea, but I have to question any points of netiquette that are based on
outdated hardware limitations.

with a crazy square mouse with one ugly button in the middle of it and
no way to even right-click. But my question is... if your draconian
newsreader is so hard to use (not yours in particular, Peter, just a
general question), why not get a better one? And if a better free
newsreader is not available, and if Google is so easy to use and full
of useful features like threading, why not use it? And no, I'm trying

"MathiasTCK" <Mathias...@gmail.com> wrote in message

>
> I know that the majority agrees. But I still don't see why. Maybe in
> the older days of usenet it was necessary.

It's still necessary. Logic, both then and now, is not to assume that
others are using any particular advanced graphic feature when reading
new. There's a number of reasons for that: personal preferences,
platform limitations, people being forced into a particular computing
environment where they might not be able to access what you can access.
Probably others I'm forgetting.

In the case of threads, there's no graphic representation I've ever
seen that works well when a thread gets large and "bushy" enough.
Including google.

> I don't trust people to quote the relevant parts anyway,

That seems a non-sequitar. What has the fear that someone else will
mess up in one way got to do with asking people not to mess up in a
different way? People should quote. AND they should quote relevant
parts of the article you're responding to.

> When it's a short response to a short post, I don't see the need.

That's actually when the need is greatest. If you don't know what
someone is replying to, there's not much you can do looking at a short
post which says nothing but, ""Me, too! I took one in the shorts, too!"
except wonder whether the person posting it has any clue what that
looked like to everyone else on the newsgroup.

> and using google groups its so easy to view the conversation as a tree.

...

> If
> whatever news group reader people are using is inferior to google
> groups in this fashion then why are they using it?

Because "whatever news group reader people are using is superior to
google in other ways. Different newsreaders have different strengths.
Google is not perfect - or everyone would use it.

> Plus depending on someone else's quotes loses track of the larger
> conversation.

It can. But if you need more context, it's _always_ easier to find
it if someone has quoted. What really deprives readers of any
sense of what's going on is when people post a quoteless answer to
a question in a large thread. Or a quoteless direct response to a
comment. If it's a generic thing he's answering or if he's confusing
about how he responds, people will never be sure what point he's trying
to make. How does THAT help anyone keep track of the larger
conversation?

> The conversation starts ignoring what people don't quote, which is
> silly.

I don't understand the comment. The conversation _always_
starts igorning whatever isn't responded to, whether it's quoted or
not. That's pretty typical: people only want to discuss the
controversial, not what they can agree on or what is really
irrelevant.

> The majority does agree though, and it is polite to follow the
> conventions of said majority in a public forum.

It really does help. You don't have to quote every word of
every sentence like I often do. Just enough to give people an
good idea of what you're responding to.

Fred

Full well indicating that the newsreader issue is the less important
issue of "why quote relevant text" (the more important being "I want
people to know what I am talking about so they will not ignore my
posts"), it isn't a matter of a better newsreader. If you read a lot of
newsgroup posts (like, say, you are LSJ, who reads them all), it is
much more convinient to have posts already read get deleted so it isn't
difficult to find new posts. Sure, you could download and archive every
post ever made just in case someone doesn't quote relevant text. Or,
you could just ignore their posts. Which do you think is more likely to
occur?

On google groups, for instance, if a thread is particularly lengthy,
finding all the new messages in a given thread takes some doing. And it
is easy to miss some. If the ones you already read weren't there
anymore, all the posts in the thread are new. No searching or figuring
out what is new.

> True, though with Google Groups, it's simply a half-flick of my finger
> on the mouse wheel. Takes less effort than scratching my ass.

Sure. But if I'm trying to communicate an idea or formulate an
argument, it is in my own best interest to make it so you don't have to
exert even that minimal effort. If I set up my discussion such that it
takes my readers effort to follow what I am saying, I am basically
saying:

A) "I'm too lazy to put the effort in so that you know what I'm talking
about--you do the extra work to have the priviledge of following my
incredibly interesting and relevant statement."

B) "Oh wait. On second thought, please ignore me."

Quoting relevant text in your discussion, regardless of actual
interface issues, is one of pure self interest. I want people to know
what I am talking about, so they will possibly pay attention. Thus, it
is in my best interest to make sure that it is easy for people to
understand what I am talking about, and quoting relevant text is one of
the best ways to do that. Much like using reasonable grammar and
punctuation.

> Though sometimes the text with no context is funnier when read on its
> own.

This is often completely true. But often completely unintentional.

-Peter

Just 'cause it seems relevant to the discussion, from the google groups
Help section on posting:

"Summarize what you're following up.

When you click "Reply" under "show options" to follow up an existing
article, Google Groups includes the full article in quotes, with the
cursor at the top of the article. Tempting though it is to just start
typing your message, please STOP and do two things first. Look at the
quoted text and remove parts that are irrelevant. Then, go to the
BOTTOM of the article and start typing there. Doing this makes it much
easier for your readers to get through your post. They'll have a
reminder of the relevant text before your comment, but won't have to
re-read the entire article. And if your reply appears on a site before
the original article does, they'll get the gist of what you're talking
about."

-Peter

I find trying to find parent posts in Google extremely difficult in
long, complex threads. This is even more complex if people have chosen
to X-no-archive their posts and I'm trying to re-read a discussion or
dig out relevant points from a set of posts in the past. Question: what
do *you* do when someone responds to an X-no-archive-d post and the post
isn't available anymore to read on Google?

Google's interface isn't perfect, and quoting helps get round most of
its imperfections. This is not just about "Click up, stupid" and
attempting to boil it down to such and rather misses the point.

I wonder how VTES players that are annoyed with the introduction of
Hunters as crypt allies would feel if such a game (WoD) was created and
its rules were similar enough to permit players to mix and match,
allowing WoD CCG Mage or Werewolf or whatever decks to contend against
VTES decks.

Of course, not every VTES playgroup would be inclined to arrange such
games (say, 4x VTES decks against a WoD werewolf deck), but I believe
most would.

But once you look closer at it, it would be not very different from
releasing VTES small sets that address the possibility as Nights of
Reckoning will do with Hunters. And still, people feel it would detract
from VTES as a "vampire game"...
